nameStory: The 'hoary' part comes from the plant's grayish-white, fuzzy appearance - hoary is an old word meaning gray or white with age, like hoarfrost. The 'tick-trefoil' part is a double warning: the seeds stick to you like ticks, and the three-leaflet pattern resembles clover (trefoil means three-leaf). So this plant literally tells you it's gray, sticky, and has three-part leaves right in its name!
description: Hoary tick-trefoil is a native wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall with a distinctly fuzzy, grayish appearance. It produces small pink to purple pea-like flowers in elongated clusters during late summer. The plant gets its common name from its three-part leaves and infamous 'stick-tight' seed pods that cling tenaciously to clothing and fur. It's part of the legume family, the same group that includes beans and peas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three oval leaflets per leaf, with the middle leaflet noticeably larger than the side ones. All surfaces feel velvety-soft due to dense, fine hairs that give the entire plant a grayish-green, almost dusty appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-shaped flowers arranged in narrow, spike-like clusters at the stem tips. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch long with the classic legume flower shape - one large top petal and smaller side and bottom petals.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive segmented seed pods that break apart into triangular sections, each covered in tiny hooked hairs that grab onto fabric and fur with remarkable tenacity. The pods are flat and jointed, resembling a string of connected triangles.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect perennial growing 2-4 feet tall with branching stems that feel slightly rough and hairy to the touch. The entire plant has a soft, grayish-fuzzy texture that makes it stand out from other wildflowers.

habitat: Look for hoary tick-trefoil in dry, open woodlands, prairie edges, and roadside areas with well-drained soils. It thrives in partially shaded spots where the forest meets open areas, often growing alongside other prairie remnant plants and oak savanna species. In New England, it's quite rare and typically found in the warmer, drier sites in the southern portions of the region.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy, three-part leaves that are noticeably soft and grayish even when young. Plants form low clumps before sending up their flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in late summer (July-August) when the spike-like clusters of small pink-purple flowers appear at stem tips, attracting various native bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: The sticky seed pods mature and readily attach to passing animals and hikers. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, leaving dried stems with persistent seed pod fragments.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems may persist with some remaining seed pod segments still clinging to the plant, though most above-ground parts die back to the perennial root system.

funFact: The hooked hairs on tick-trefoil seed pods are so effective that they inspired part of the design for Velcro - nature perfected this 'hook and loop' fastening system millions of years before humans thought to copy it!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tick-trefoils, but hoary tick-trefoil's distinctly fuzzy, grayish appearance sets it apart from its relatives. Remember: if it looks like someone dusted the entire plant with gray powder and it feels notably soft and velvety, you've found the hoary one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the 'tick' in its name, this plant has nothing to do with the blood-sucking arachnids we worry about. The name refers purely to how the seeds 'tick' or stick to things. However, the irony is that the brushy areas where tick-trefoils grow are often exactly where you might encounter real ticks!
compareHints: Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable. Showy tick-trefoil is much taller and greener, while panicled tick-trefoil has branched flower clusters rather than simple spikes. The soft, velvety texture and dusty gray-green color of hoary tick-trefoil is unique in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
